content.title: About
content.content: Chicken breast cooked on a rotisserie with the skin eaten is a tender source of protein obtained by slowly rotating the meat over heat. This method retains juices, while the skin becomes crispy and flavorful.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: A rotisserie grill allows even cooking thanks to constant rotation of the meat.
Chicken skin contains more fat than the breast itself, but during proper cooking some fat melts, enhancing flavor.
Rotisserie chicken is a tradition popular in the Mediterranean and the Middle East.
Typical rotisserie temperatures range from 180‑200 °C, producing a golden crust.
Boneless chicken breast cooks faster than bone‑in but retains a high nutrient density.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Chicken breast provides about 31 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: The product contains virtually no carbs, making it suitable for low‑carb diets.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Chicken is high in niacin (B3) and vitamin B6, which are essential for energy metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: It supplies phosphorus, selenium and zinc, important for bones, immunity and antioxidant protection.

items.title: Low fat (without skin)
items.content: Removing the skin reduces fat to about 3‑4 g per 100 g, fitting diets that limit fat intake.

items.title: Chicken allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to chicken proteins.

items.title: Fat content in skin
items.content: Chicken skin is high in saturated fat; excessive consumption may raise cholesterol levels.

items.title: Bacterial contamination risk
items.content: Undercooked meat can harbor Salmonella; ensure internal temperature reaches 75 °C.

items.title: Sodium in marinades
items.content: Rotisserie chicken is often marinated with salt; people with hypertension should monitor intake.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Rotisserie chicken breast can be eaten hot, sliced into salads, sandwiches, or added to pasta dishes. The skin can be left for crunch or removed to reduce fat.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked chicken breast in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in a bag at –18 °C, where it keeps quality for 2‑3 months. Reheat to an internal temperature of 75 °C before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Tilapia is a freshwater fish from the cichlid family, widely farmed in aquaculture. Grilled, it has a delicate, slightly sweet flavor and a firm yet tender texture. Tilapia is often used in salads, rice dishes, and as a light source of protein.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Tilapia is one of the fastest‑growing farmed fish, reaching market size in 6‑8 months.
The species tolerates a wide range of water conditions, including low oxygen levels.
Its mild taste makes it an excellent canvas for marinades and spices.
Globally, over 5 million tonnes of tilapia are produced each year, making it one of the most popular fish species.
Tilapia can thrive in water temperatures from 15 °C to 30 °C.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: A 100‑g serving provides about 20 g of high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Tilapia is a lean fish, suitable for calorie‑controlled diets.

items.title: Contains vitamin B12
items.content: Vitamin B12 supports nervous system function and red blood cell formation.

items.title: Source of selenium
items.content: Selenium acts as an antioxidant and helps maintain immune health.

items.title: Provides essential minerals
items.content: Tilapia supplies phosphorus, potassium and magnesium, important for bone and muscle health.

items.title: Water quality control
items.content: In some regions tilapia may be raised in water with higher contaminant levels; choose products from reputable sources.

items.title: Fish allergy
items.content: People allergic to seafood may react to tilapia as well.

items.title: Omega‑6 fatty acids
items.content: Tilapia contains more omega‑6 than omega‑3 fatty acids, so balance the diet with other omega‑3 sources.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Grilled tilapia pairs well with lemon, herbs, garlic, or pesto sauce. It can be sliced for salads, added to pasta, rice dishes, or used in sandwiches.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fresh tilapia in the refrigerator at 0‑2 °C, wrapped in plastic film, for up to 2 days. Frozen fillets keep at –18 °C for up to 3 months. Discard if it develops an off‑odor.

rice-white-with-vegetables-cheese-and-or.title: White rice with vegetables and cheese and/or cream sauce, fat added

content.title: About
content.content: This dish consists of boiled white rice, sautéed vegetables (such as carrots, broccoli, bell pepper) and a sauce made from cheese and/or cream with added fat. It combines carbohydrates, vegetable vitamins and minerals, as well as saturated fats that give the dish a creamy texture and rich flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: White rice is a primary source of energy due to its high starch content.
Vegetables retain most of their vitamins and fiber when steamed or quickly stir‑fried.
Cheese and cream add not only taste but also calcium, important for bone health.
The added fat enhances absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) from the vegetables.
The dish is common in Asian and Mediterranean cuisines as a hearty lunch or dinner.

items.title: Energy supply
items.content: Rice provides a rapid source of glucose needed for maintaining energy levels.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals from vegetables
items.content: Vegetables are rich in vitamin C, vitamin K, folate, and potassium, supporting immunity and heart function.

items.title: Calcium from cheese and cream
items.content: Calcium is essential for bone and tooth health and participates in muscle contraction.

items.title: Fat for better nutrient absorption
items.content: Saturated and monounsaturated fats help the body absorb fat‑soluble vitamins.

items.title: Protein
items.content: Cheese and a modest amount of cream contribute dairy protein, aiding tissue repair.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: The dish contains a notable amount of fats and carbs, so portion control is advisable, especially on weight‑loss diets.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: Cheese and cream may cause discomfort for people who are lactose intolerant.

items.title: Sodium level
items.content: If the sauce is seasoned with salt, the dish can be high in sodium, which is undesirable for hypertension.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to cheese or cream.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish hot, often as a main course. It pairs well with fresh herbs, a squeeze of lemon, or soy sauce for extra flavor. For added protein, include chicken breast or tofu.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. When reheating, add a splash of water or milk to prevent the sauce from becoming too thick.

content.title: About
content.content: Reduced‑sodium canned bean soup is a ready‑to‑eat soup made from selected dry beans, vegetables, and spices. The canning process preserves flavor and nutrients while significantly lowering added salt.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Beans are one of the oldest cultivated legumes, grown by humans for over 7,000 years.
Canning allows the product to be stored for 2‑3 years without quality loss.
Sodium reduction is achieved by using natural flavor enhancers and spices instead of salt.
Bean soup is considered a comfort food in many cultures, from the United States to Russia.
Legumes are rich in plant protein and fiber, making them an excellent choice for vegetarians.

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: Beans provide about 8 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion and helps maintain stable blood‑sugar levels.

items.title: Low sodium content
items.content: Reduced salt is beneficial for individuals monitoring blood pressure.

items.title: Source of iron and magnesium
items.content: These minerals contribute to hemoglobin formation and nervous system function.

items.title: Supports immunity
items.content: B‑vitamins and antioxidants in beans help strengthen the immune system.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: Some people may experience allergic reactions to beans.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Certain recipes may add sugar or sweeteners; diabetics should check the label.

items.title: Preservatives
items.content: While most brands avoid artificial preservatives, some may use additives that cause sensitivity.

items.title: Proper heating
items.content: The soup should be heated to a rolling boil to eliminate any possible bacteria.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat the soup in the microwave or on the stove for about 5‑7 minutes. It can be garnished with fresh herbs, served with crusty bread, or paired with boiled potatoes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the unopened can in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, transfer leftovers to an airtight container and keep refrigerated for up to 3‑4 days.
